summary: This document defines common YANG types and groupings for scheduling events, policies, services or resources by date and time. It includes recurrence-related groupings at varying levels of detail.

eli5.summary: A shared calendar template for network settings, saying when things should happen and how often.

questions: what is the ietf-schedule yang module
subtitle: A shared YANG module of building blocks for describing when things happen and how often they repeat.

tldr.problem: Many YANG models need to say when something should happen, such as an event, policy, service or resource, and each would otherwise invent its own date and time representation.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-schedule module defines reusable groupings: validation guards, a period of time, recurrence rules from basic to iCalendar-like, and status reporting, plus identities and two features.
tldr.outcome: Other modules can import these groupings instead of redefining them. The module itself exposes no writable data nodes, read-only state or RPCs.

today: RFC 9922 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2026 and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 9922 defines a common ietf-schedule YANG module of reusable groupings for scheduling events, policies, services or resources based on date and time. Other documents it names as possible users include network access control, OAM and a scheduling model. It also defines groupings for validating requested schedules and reporting scheduling statuses.

The RFC makes no assumption about what the scheduled actions do. Detection and resolution of schedule conflicts are out of scope. The appendices give examples of each grouping, sample modules showing how to use and extend the module, and an example for a scheduled-use-of-resources framework (RFC 8413).
sections.eli5: It is a box of calendar building blocks. It does not decide what happens at the scheduled time. It only says when.

sections.title: Types, Identities and Features
sections.content:
The module defines four identity families. schedule-type has three values: one-shot (zero duration, or end equal to start, after which the schedule disables itself), period (a start and end, or a start and positive duration, lasting forever if neither is given) and recurrence (periodic, such as every five minutes, or irregular, such as every day at 8 and 9 AM).

frequency-type gives the repeat unit (secondly, minutely, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly). schedule-state gives the status, such as enabled, disabled, conflicted, finished or out-of-date. discard-action-type says what to do when a request is discarded: warning, error or silently-discard.

Two features let implementations choose how much recurrence they support: basic-recurrence and icalendar-recurrence. Which of them is supported is implementation specific.
sections.eli5: The module has lists of words for the kind of schedule, how often it repeats, whether it is on, and what to do with a bad request. A device can say it only understands the simple calendar or the fancy one.

sections.title: Guards and Periods
sections.content:
The generic-schedule-params grouping holds guards a system applies to all schedules: validity, max-allowed-start, min-allowed-start, max-allowed-end, a time-zone-identifier, a description and a discard-action. A request is rejected if its first occurrence starts outside the allowed start bounds or its last occurrence ends after max-allowed-end. Occurrences starting after validity are not executed. The time zone identifier MUST be given if any value is in local time and MUST NOT be applied to UTC or offset values.

The period-of-time grouping describes one period with a period-start and either a period-end or a duration. The start MUST be no later than the end. With no end or duration the period lasts forever, and with no start it begins immediately.
sections.eli5: These are the rules at the door: how early or late a schedule may start, and when it must be over. A plain period is just a start and an end.

sections.title: The Recurrence Groupings
sections.content:
Recurrence is offered in layers. recurrence-basic is a simple rule that starts immediately and repeats forever, built from a frequency and an interval; for example, a daily rule with interval 8 means every eight days. recurrence-utc adds a first occurrence (start-time-utc and duration in seconds) and an end given either by an until time or a count, which MUST be greater than 1. It is aimed at machine readability. recurrence-with-time-zone is the same idea with a time zone, aimed at human readability.

The two with-periods variants add a list of extra periods, and the occurrences are the union of the rule and the list, with duplicates ignored. In the UTC variant the list uses yang:timeticks from RFC 9911.

icalendar-recurrence builds on the time-zone variant and adds iCalendar-like nodes from RFC 5545: bysecond, byminute, byhour, byday, bymonthday, byyearday, byyearweek, byyearmonth, bysetpos, workweek-start and exception-dates. For example, in a monthly rule, a byday of monday with direction -1 is the last Monday of the month. Exception dates are removed from the final set.

The basic groupings deliberately define no default or mandatory, so using modules SHOULD refine frequency and interval as needed.
sections.eli5: You can pick a simple repeat, like every 8 days, or a detailed one, like the last Monday of every month. You can also list days to skip, like holidays.

sections.title: Status Reporting and Usage Rules
sections.content:
The schedule-status grouping, with variants adding a time zone or a schedule-name, exposes state, version, schedule-type and read-only local-time, last-update, counter, last-occurrence, upcoming-occurrence, last-failed-occurrence and failure-counter. The counter and occurrence nodes are only available for the recurrence type. Unless something resets it, the failure counter is reset only when the schedule starts.

Section 4 adds usage restrictions. Period start MUST be before period end, dates MUST be valid, and the seconds value SHOULD be 60 at the end of months with a leap second unless time sync ignores leap seconds. Schedules whose start is in the past SHOULD be ignored, although local policy MAY let an implementation skip past occurrences and start from the next match.
sections.eli5: A schedule can also report how it is doing: is it on, when did it last run, when does it run next, and how many times did it fail?

sections.title: Relation to the DISMAN-SCHEDULE-MIB
sections.content: RFC 3231 defined a MIB for scheduling management operations. RFC 9922 defines no data nodes for this purpose but gives a table mapping the main MIB objects to YANG parameters. For example, schedLocalTime maps to local-time, schedType to schedule-type, schedInterval to interval and schedAdminStatus to state. Two objects, schedOwner and schedContextName, are not supported.
sections.eli5: An older system already had scheduling. This RFC shows which old setting matches which new one, so you can move across.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module only defines identities, types and groupings, with no writable data nodes, read-only state or RPCs of its own, so the RFC finds no additional security issues for the module itself. Modules that use the groupings should identify their own considerations. The RFC lists these concerns: scheduling depends on accurate time synchronization; recurring events may hide abnormal behavior; missing logs of each occurrence make incidents hard to trace; and very frequent recurrences can keep a system busy managing schedules.

The IANA actions register the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-schedule and the YANG module name ietf-schedule with prefix schedule.
sections.eli5: The calendar blocks are safe by themselves. The risk is in how others use them, for example a wrong clock or a schedule that fires so often the device is always busy.
